Extraction: A Practical Approach to Defining a Framework for Developing an Agentic AIOps System
Răzvan Daniel Zota; Corneliu Bărbulescu; Radu Constantinescu

Conventional AIOps systems are limited to observability and predefined rules with reactive responses, lacking autonomy to proactively detect and resolve incidents without human input; critical tasks such as incident resolution and problem management still require significant human intervention, and there is no canonical definition of Agentic AIOps (Sec. 1, pp. 1-3).

A three-dimensional development framework for an Agentic AIOps system: (1) process model dimension aligned with ITIL via IBM's UPF-IT/PRM-IT (Event Management, Service Execution, Request Fulfillment, Incident Management, Problem Management); (2) service element dimension (applications, platform/middleware, infrastructure); (3) capability dimension following the Understand-Decide-Take Action paradigm; an Orchestrator component controls flow across components: discriminative AI for incident classification, RAG for diagnosis, automation components (e.g., Jenkins pipeline, Ansible playbook) for resolution, and an AI-LLM component for closure communication; autonomy is deployed progressively across ten levels with human oversight at critical decision points (Sec. 4.1-4.3, pp. 11-16; Sec. 3.1, p. 9).

Conceptual framework proposal (vision paper) grounded in: a systematic literature review of academic articles, industry reports and white papers from the last five years (140+ articles filtered to 42 high-impact studies); the authors' own IT industry experience (IBM UPF-IT, Watson AIOps, Splunk); and focus group discussions plus semi-structured interviews with IT professionals, AI researchers, and AIOps practitioners; no prototype, deployment, or experimental evaluation (Sec. 2.1-2.4, pp. 4-5).

Not specified quantitatively — no baselines or measured values reported; qualitative claims only: the authors state such a system "can significantly reduce incident response time" and enable self-healing IT environments, and Table 2 lists "Reduce Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR)" as the end goal of AIOps (Abstract, p. 1; Table 2, p. 7).

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: No empirical efficacy results; the framework contributes design principles for reliable autonomy: progressive autonomy over ten defined levels matched to risk tolerance, process standardization via ITIL/UPF-IT, service-aware design across layers, continuous learning feedback loops, and human oversight for high-risk actions; an orchestrator manages end-to-end control flow across specialized AI/automation components; the paper also proposes a definition of Agentic AIOps as agents operating at different levels of autonomy (Sec. 4.3, pp. 14-16; Sec. 4, p. 11; Sec. 3.1, p. 9).

Authors acknowledge "currently we do not have experimental results that materialize the presented view" (vision of the future of Agentic AIOps) and that security concerns are out of scope; future work: defining system capabilities per ITIL Operations process, specifying components per technology (infrastructure, middleware, application), and proposing a conceptual architecture; ethical/governance considerations (accountability, transparency, oversight, KPI monitoring) are flagged as needing attention (Sec. 5, pp. 16-17).

This paper provides a structured conceptual foundation for positioning an Agentic AI copilot within incident response: its Understand-Decide-Take Action paradigm and the incident management mapping (classification, RAG-based diagnosis, automated resolution, LLM-based closure) mirror the pipeline a copilot would support to reduce MTTD and MTTR. The ten-level autonomy scale and progressive-autonomy principle offer a vocabulary for characterizing the copilot (human-in-the-loop) versus fully autonomous operation. Its alignment with ITIL/UPF-IT grounds the thesis in service management practice. However, it offers no empirical MTTD/MTTR evidence, so it serves as a framing and architecture reference rather than a source of quantitative benchmarks.
Medium — directly proposes an agentic AIOps framework for autonomous incident detection, diagnosis, and resolution, but it is purely conceptual and reports no MTTD/MTTR measurements.
